diagrams.title: Access Control Models Matrix
diagrams.subtitle: Who decides, on what basis, and for how long? Six models from §4.5, five of which are outside the books.

cells.detail: The resource owner grants or revokes access at their discretion.
An authority defines labels and rules: even the owner cannot override them.
Permissions are attached to a role and inherited by users assigned to it.
Explicit rules (ACL, IP range, allowlist) apply to everyone.
A time window or expiration date determines authorization.
An approved request triggers a time-limited elevation.
Flexible but hard to audit: permissions propagate without central control.
Classification and "need to know": a strict model suited to sensitive environments.
Dominant enterprise model: easy to audit, grant, and revoke.
Rule applied uniformly, regardless of identity or role.
Business hours, assignment duration, contract end date.
Short duration, often a few hours, with automatic revocation.
DAC = flexibility, but the owner can pass permissions on without central visibility.
MAC applies even against the owner: this is the criterion that distinguishes it from DAC.
Removing the user from the role removes all their permissions: that is the strength of RBAC.
Rule-based applies to everyone indiscriminately, unlike DAC.
Time-based plans the end of access right from assignment.
JIT reduces the time during which an elevated privilege is active.
